statement.p: Consider the integral \displaystyle \int\,2\,x^{3}\,(x^{4} + 1)\,dx. In the following, we will evaluate the integral using two methods.
A. First, rewrite the integral by multiplying out the integrand:
Then evaluate the resulting integral term-by-term:
B. Next, rewrite the integral using the substitution w = x^{4} + 1:
Evaluate this integral (and back-substitute for w) to find the value of the original integral:
C. How are your expressions from parts (A) and (B) different? What is the difference between the two? (Ignore the constant of integration.)
Are both of the answers correct? (Be sure you can explain why they are!)

static.solution:
A. \int\,2\,x^{3}\,(x^{4} + 1)\,dx = \int\,2\,x^{7} + 2\,x^{3}\,dx. Thus, antidifferentiating term-by-term, we get \int\,2\,x^{3}\,(x^{4} + 1)\,dx = {1\over4}\,x^{8} + {1\over2}\,x^{4} + C.
B. \int\,2\,x^{3}\,(x^{4} + 1)\,dx = \int\,{1\over2}\,w\,dw. Thus, antidifferentiating, we get \int\,2\,x^{3}\,(x^{4} + 1)\,dx = {1\over4}\,w^2 + C = {1\over4}\,(x^{4} + 1)^2 + C.
C. To see the difference between these two answers, we expand the second: (x^{4} + 1)^2 = x^{8} + 2\,x^{4} + 1, so the difference is ({1\over4} (x^{8} + 2\,x^{4} + 1)) - ({1\over4} \,x^{8} + {1\over2}\,x^{4}) = {1\over4}. That is, the difference is a constant! This is completely reasonable: the antiderivative is only determined up to a constant, and the arbitrary constant C that we get for the most general antiderivative will adjust for this difference.
